questions.prompt: You have 90 minutes before committee on a complex multi-entity deal with conflicting income signals. Which sequence is closest to the capstone workflow?
choices: Prompt AI for a memo skeleton first to anchor your thinking, then read the file to fill in the details, then write the recommendation

Read the file fully first, decide your tentative call, redact once, then use AI in three constrained passes (capital structure, income signals, risk/mitigant expansion), then write your own reconciliation and recommendation, then verify all numbers, then fair-lending review
Redact and feed the entire file to AI in a single prompt asking for a complete committee memo, then edit the output to match your voice
Skip the AI synthesis on a 90-minute deadline; AI saves time on simple deals but adds overhead on complex ones
questions.explanation: The capstone is explicit on order. Reading first forms the gestalt. Deciding a tentative call anchors the synthesis. Redacting once is faster than three times. AI runs in constrained synthesis passes only — not as a memo-generator. Reconciliation and recommendation are yours. Verification and fair-lending review are non-negotiable. The first option inverts the order in a way that lets the model's framing shape your call. The third turns the model into the underwriter. The fourth is wrong — AI saves more time on complex deals than on simple ones, when used correctly.

questions.prompt: On the same deal, you finish your AI-assisted draft with 10 minutes to spare. Two final tasks compete for that time: (a) verify every dollar figure in the memo against source documents, or (b) re-read the memo end-to-end as if you were the committee chair. Which is the correct prioritization?
choices: Do (b) first — committee will read it cold and the holistic read catches the most issues
Do (a) first — unverified numbers in front of committee is the single largest reputational and audit risk in the whole workflow
Skip both — the work is good enough after the AI passes; over-checking costs more than it saves
Do (a) but only for the largest figures — small numbers are within rounding tolerance
questions.explanation: Verification is the load-bearing step that makes the synthesis steps safe. An unverified number from the model can be entirely fabricated. The holistic read is important and the capstone includes it as a separate step, but if forced to choose, verification comes first because the failure mode is more severe. The fourth option is wrong because the small figures (e.g., a $4k monthly debt service swing on a refinance) are often the load-bearing ones for the credit call.

questions.prompt: Reviewing your finished memo, you find a sentence in the risk section that reads: 'Furthermore, from a credit perspective, the obligor's profile reflects a measured approach to leverage.' You did not write that sentence. What is the right interpretation and action?
choices: The sentence is fine — it is neutral, plausibly true, and adds polish to the section

The sentence is AI residue — generic transitional phrasing, hedged characterization, and a sentiment that softens rather than describes; rewrite or cut it because it is not your voice and not your judgment
Keep the sentence but add a citation to a specific data point that supports the 'measured approach to leverage' claim
Keep the sentence as a hedge; if anything goes wrong with the deal, the language gives you defensible ground
questions.explanation: This is the AI-residue check from the capstone. The model has a voice — 'furthermore,' 'from a credit perspective,' soft characterizations like 'measured approach' — that does not belong in a Kapitus committee memo. Adding a citation tries to rescue a sentence that should not be there. Treating hedged language as defensive cover is exactly the wrong instinct: vague language is harder to defend than specific language, both at committee and on audit. Cut it.
